promise_band.headline: Winter weather doesn't stop us
promise_band.body: In northeastern Pennsylvania the roof problems arrive in January. Ice builds at the eaves, meltwater backs up under the shingles, and the stain shows up on a bedroom ceiling three days later — usually right when half the contractors in the valley have shut down until spring. We work through it. Call us in February and you will get a person, an appointment and a straight answer about whether it is an ice dam, a flashing failure, or a roof that has simply run out of years.

signature_system.headline: What actually happens on your roof
signature_system.intro: Roofing is not complicated, but it is easy to do badly in ways a homeowner never sees. Here is what we do, and why each part matters once the old shingles are off.

blocks.title: We strip it to the deck and look
blocks.body: Layering new shingles over old hides everything worth finding. We tear off to the bare decking, then walk it. Soft boards, rot around the chimney, split rafters — that is the moment those get found, not two winters later when the ceiling stains.

blocks.title: Bad decking gets replaced, not covered
blocks.body: Fasteners only hold as well as the wood they go into. Anything soft or delaminated comes out and new sheathing goes down before a single course of underlayment. It is the least visible part of the job and the part a cheap quote quietly skips.

blocks.title: Water barrier first, shingles second
blocks.body: Ice-and-water membrane at the eaves and in the valleys, then underlayment across the field, then flashing worked properly into the chimney and sidewalls. In a climate that freezes and thaws all winter, this layer is what actually keeps the water out — the shingles are the part you can see.

blocks.title: Then we clean up like it is our own house
blocks.body: Debris into the dumpster as it comes off, a rolling magnet across the lawn, the driveway and the flowerbeds, and a walk of the property before the truck moves. Nails in the grass is the single most common complaint homeowners have about roofers. Our reviews say it is not one of ours.

signature_system.steps_title: What that looks like on your calendar

steps.title: Free estimate, in writing
steps.body: We come out, get on the roof, and give you a written number — not a range shouted from the driveway.

steps.title: We schedule around the weather
steps.body: Materials get delivered, and we give you a date. NEPA weather moves; if it moves the date, you hear it from us first.

steps.title: Tear-off and install, usually one day
steps.body: A typical Scranton house goes from old roof to new roof between morning and evening.

steps.title: Cleanup and walkthrough
steps.body: Magnet pass, property walk, and we do not leave until you have looked at it.

guarantee.title: If it is our work, we come back
guarantee.body: Every roofing job hits something unexpected — that is the nature of pulling the lid off a house. What separates contractors is what happens after. If a leak traces back to our workmanship, we come back and we fix it. One customer has now had us out for a third and fourth roof over five years. That does not happen if you do not stand behind the first one.

about_block.headline: Independent, family owned, and from around here
about_block.body: We are an independent, family owned business that came out of a small local town, and we work in the communities we live in. We take pride in treating each home as if it were our own — as homeowners ourselves, we know what weather damage costs and what it feels like to worry about it. The memories made in a home are a treasure, and protecting them is the part of this job that matters.

seo_body.headline: What a Scranton roof is actually up against
paragraphs: Scranton housing stock is old and it is dense. Double blocks and row homes sharing a wall, steep slate roofs from the coal era, back porches and additions running flat against the main pitch, and chimneys that have been reflashed by three different people over sixty years. It is not a market where one roof system fits every house — which is why we run asphalt, slate, metal and four different flat-roof membranes rather than selling everyone the same package.

The weather does the rest. Northeastern Pennsylvania freezes and thaws all winter long, and that cycle is what actually kills roofs here. Snow melts off the warm middle of a roof, refreezes at the cold eave, and the resulting ice dam pushes water backwards under the shingles where no shingle was ever designed to stop it. That is why we put ice-and-water membrane at the eaves and in every valley as a matter of course, and why we do not shut the phones off in January the way a lot of contractors in the valley do.

The other thing worth knowing: Pennsylvania does not issue a roofing license. Registration with the Attorney General's office confirms a contractor carries insurance — it certifies nothing about the quality of the work, and the state's lookup database has spent long stretches offline. So homeowners here are left doing what homeowners have always done, which is asking a neighbor. We would rather be judged on that than on a badge. Seventy-four Google reviews, an average of 4.6, and customers who have had us back for a third and fourth roof is the record we would point at.
checklist: Free estimate, delivered in writing after we get on the roof
Tear-off to the deck — bad sheathing replaced, not covered over
Ice-and-water membrane at the eaves and valleys as standard
Flat and low-slope roofs: EPDM, TPO, torch-down and peel-and-stick
Magnet sweep and a property walk before the truck leaves

faqs.q: What does an estimate cost, and how fast can I get one?
faqs.a: Nothing, and quickly. We come out, get on the roof rather than eyeballing it from the driveway, and give you the number in writing. Customers specifically mention how fast the estimate came back — not having to chase a contractor for a price is half the reason people call us in the first place.

faqs.q: How long does a roof replacement take?
faqs.a: Most residential roofs in this area are a one-day job once the material is on site. Reviewers say it themselves: "My new roof was on in one day." Bigger homes, steep slate work and roofs that turn up rotted decking can run into a second day, and we tell you that up front rather than at the end.

faqs.q: Do you work in the winter?
faqs.a: Yes. Northeastern Pennsylvania does most of its roof damage between December and March, so shutting down for the season never made sense to us. Ice dams, wind-lifted shingles and flashing leaks all get handled through the winter, and we are reachable seven days a week.

faqs.q: My ceiling is stained but I cannot see anything wrong from the ground. What now?
faqs.a: Water travels. The stain is almost never directly under the entry point, which is why guessing at a patch usually fails. We trace it properly — chimney and sidewall flashing, valleys, vent boots and ice-dam backup at the eaves are the usual suspects on Scranton houses, in roughly that order. You get photos of whatever we find.

faqs.q: Do I need a full replacement, or can this be repaired?
faqs.a: Plenty of roofs we look at have years left and need a flashing detail fixed, not a tear-off. We will tell you when that is the case. A roof at the end of its life shows it — granules gone, shingles curling and brittle, multiple leaks in different planes — and at that point repairs stop being economical. Either way you get the reasoning, with photos.

faqs.q: My roof is flat. Do you do those?
faqs.a: Yes, residential and commercial. Scranton has a lot of flat and low-slope roofs — back additions, porch roofs, small commercial buildings — and we run all four common membranes: EPDM rubber, TPO, torch-down modified bitumen and peel-and-stick. Which one is right depends on the deck, the drainage and how much foot traffic the roof gets.

faqs.q: Can you match or repair a slate roof?
faqs.a: We do work on slate, including full slate installation, and we also install slate-like architectural shingles for homeowners who want the look without the cost or the weight. Older Scranton homes with original slate are worth an honest conversation about which way to go — the two paths are very different in price and lifespan.

faqs.q: What about the deposit and payment schedule?
faqs.a: Ask us directly and we will put it in writing with the estimate before anything is signed. Homeowners are right to be cautious here — stories about large deposits and disappearing contractors are common, and nothing about a payment schedule should be verbal.

Roofing is messy while it is happening; that part is unavoidable. What is avoidable is what gets left behind. Debris goes into the dumpster as it comes off, a rolling magnet goes over the lawn, driveway and beds, and someone walks the property before we pull out. Three separate Google reviewers brought up our cleanup without being asked.

We are based at 614 N Rebecca Ave in West Scranton and work across Lackawanna and Luzerne counties — Scranton, Dunmore, Dickson City, Old Forge, Clarks Summit and Wilkes-Barre, plus the surrounding boroughs. If you are not sure whether you are in range, call and ask.
